questions.question: How do you create a regular expression in JavaScript?
What does the test method do on a regex?
questions.answer:
The test method returns true when the pattern matches anywhere in the string and false otherwise.

code:
console.log(/\d+/.test('price 42'));  // true
console.log(/\d+/.test('abc'));       // false

real example:
Asserting a response body matches an expected shape uses regex.test on values before deeper extraction.

questions.question: What is the difference between test, exec, and match?
questions.answer:
test returns a boolean, exec returns detailed match arrays with capture groups, and match is the string method that does the same for the string.

code:
const m = /(\d+)-(\d+)/.exec('order-12-45');
console.log(m[1]);   // 12
console.log('12-45'.match(/(\d+)/)[1]);  // 12

real example:
Extracting the id from a URL route with exec gives the integer group used in a follow-up API request.

questions.question: What do the g, i, and m flags do?
questions.answer:
g makes the search global so match returns all occurrences, i makes matching case-insensitive, and m makes ^ and $ match per line instead of the whole string.

code:
console.log('a b a'.match(/a/g).length);  // 2
console.log(/login/i.test('LOGIN'));      // true

real example:
Case-insensitive text equality in Cypress like expect(text).to.match(/successfully/i) ignores case and punctuation variance.

questions.question: What do anchors ^ and $ mean in a regex?
questions.answer:
^ anchors the match to the start of the string and $ anchors it to the end, so /^abc$/ matches exactly abc and nothing longer.

code:
console.log(/^done$/.test('done'));    // true
console.log(/^done$/.test('done!'));   // false

real example:
Enforcing exact status text like successful login uses anchors so partial matches never pass an assertion.

questions.question: What are character classes such as \d, \w, and \s?
questions.answer:
\d matches any digit, \w any word character, and \s any whitespace. Their uppercase forms match the negation.

code:
const re = /^\w{3}\d{2}$/;
console.log(re.test('abc12'));  // true

real example:
Validating phone and zip formats before posting to an API uses character classes in the pattern.

questions.question: How do quantifiers like *, +, and ? work?
questions.answer:
* matches zero or more, + matches one or more, and ? matches zero or one of the preceding token, controlling repetition by default greedily.

code:
console.log(/a+/.test(''));        // false
console.log(/a*/.test(''));        // true
console.log(/colou?r/.test('color')); // true

real example:
Tax and currency parsing tolerances like optional spaces or decimal parts rely on ? quantifiers.

questions.question: What is a capture group and how do you use it?
questions.answer:
A capture group is a parenthesized part of the pattern that is stored separately, accessible by index from exec or match results.

code:
const m = 'order-5533'.match(/order-(\d+)/);
console.log(m[1]);  // 5533

real example:
Extracting a numeric order id from confirmation text then using it in a database lookup is a classic capture-group task.

questions.question: How do you replace text using a regex?
What is the difference between the literal and the RegExp constructor?
questions.answer:
The literal /pattern/ is static and compiled once, while new RegExp('pattern') builds from a string, which is necessary for patterns generated at runtime.

code:
const prefix = 'product-';
const re = new RegExp('^' + prefix + '\\d+$');
console.log(re.test('product-42'));  // true
console.log(re.test('product-abc')); // false

real example:
Building a validator for dynamic prefixes keeps the pattern parametrized while escaping user-provided search terms prevents regex injection.

questions.question: How do you use a regex in a Playwright assertion?
What does a lookahead like (?=...) do?
questions.answer:
A lookahead asserts that the pattern inside exists ahead without including it in the match, enabling complex password and format validations.

code:
const strong = /^(?=.*[A-Z])(?=.*\d).+$/;
console.log(strong.test('Ab1'));  // true

real example:
Signup form validation checks (uppercase plus digit) are commonly encoded as lookaheads asserted by the test.

questions.question: What does the . (dot) match and how do you match a literal dot?
questions.answer:
The dot matches any single character except a newline by default. To match an actual dot or any metacharacter literally, escape it with a backslash.

code:
console.log(/a.b/.test('acb'));  // true
console.log(/a\.b/.test('a.b')); // true

real example:
Parsing version strings like 1.2.3 requires escaped dots, otherwise any character wrongly satisfies the pattern.

questions.question: How do you create a regex to match an email address?
questions.answer:
A practical pattern uses character classes and escaped symbols, though perfect RFC email validation in one line is unrealistic.

code:
const email = /^[\w.+-]+@[\w-]+\.[\w.]+$/;
console.log(email.test('user+test@example.com'));  // true

real example:
Asserting server responses contain valid email addresses uses the same pattern to reject obvious malformed values.

questions.question: Why is the global flag required for matchAll or replace all?
questions.answer:
matchAll and global replace operate across the entire string, so an inner regex without g matches only the first occurrence.

code:
const all = 'a1b2'.matchAll(/\d/g);
console.log([...all].map(m => m[0]));  // ['1', '2']

real example:
Counting occurrences of a tag in raw HTML uses a global regex; relying on non-global patterns under-counts matches in tests.
